rule.summary: Every German noun has a grammatical gender: masculine (**der**), feminine (**die**) or neuter (**das**). The gender belongs to the word, not to the thing or person: *das Mädchen, die Person, der Löffel, die Gabel, das Messer*. In the plural all nouns take **die**. In this topic the noun is the subject or stands after *sein* (Nominativ); in other cases the article changes (*den, dem, des*), which you learn in later topics. Always learn a new noun together with its article and its plural.
rule.table:
| Genus | Artikel (Nom.) | Gute Hinweise | Beispiele |
|---|---|---|---|
| maskulin | **der** | männliche Personen; Tage, Monate, Jahreszeiten; viele Wetterwörter; *-ling, -ismus, -ist*; Geräte auf *-er* | der Vater, der Montag, der Winter, der Tourist, der Computer |
| feminin | **die** | weibliche Personen, *-in*; *-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ei, -ik, -thek*; viele Nomen auf *-e* | die Ärztin, die Zeitung, die Lektion, die Bäckerei, die Lampe |
| neutral | **das** | *-chen, -lein*; Infinitive als Nomen; *-um, -ment*; viele Wörter mit *Ge-* | das Mädchen, das Essen, das Museum, das Gemüse |
| Plural | **die** | alle drei Genera | die Männer, die Frauen, die Kinder |
steps: Learn every noun as a unit: article + noun + plural (*der Tisch, -e*; *die Lampe, -n*; *das Buch, ¨-er*).
Look at the ending first. Suffixes are the most reliable clue: *-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät* → *die*; *-chen, -lein* → *das*; *-ling, -ismus* → *der*.
For a compound noun, take the gender of the **last** part: *das Haus + die Tür → die Haustür*; *kühl + der Schrank → der Kühlschrank*.

For people, the article usually follows the natural gender (*der Vater, die Mutter*); *-in* makes a feminine form (*der Lehrer → die Lehrerin*). Learn the exceptions: *das Mädchen, das Kind, die Person*.
If the noun is plural, the Nominativ article is always *die*, whatever the singular gender: *der Mann → die Männer, das Kind → die Kinder*.
Use *der/die/das* when the noun is the subject or after *sein*. As an object or after a preposition the form changes (*den, dem, des*).
pitfalls: Choosing the article by the real sex of a person: ✗ *die Mädchen* (for one girl) → ✓ *das Mädchen*; ✗ *der Person* → ✓ *die Person*.
Taking the gender of the first part of a compound: ✗ *das Hausaufgabe* (because of *das Haus*) → ✓ *die Hausaufgabe*.

Thinking every noun in *-er* is masculine: ✗ *der Wasser, der Fenster* → ✓ *das Wasser, das Fenster*. The *-er* clue is reliable only for people and devices (*der Lehrer, der Drucker*); other *-er* nouns must be learned one by one.
Thinking every noun in *-e* is feminine: ✗ *die Käse* → ✓ *der Käse*; also *der Name, das Auge*.
Keeping the singular article in the plural: ✗ *das Kinder* → ✓ *die Kinder*; ✗ *der Schlüssel* (for several keys) → ✓ *die Schlüssel*.

items.explanation: *Hund* is masculine: **der Hund**. For animals the gender cannot be guessed from the meaning: *der Hund*, but *die Katze* and *das Pferd*. *Der Hund* is the subject, so the Nominativ form **Der** is used.

mistake.why: *Hund* is not neuter. Nothing in the word shows the gender, so it must be learned as *der Hund*.

examples.en: The bird is singing in the garden.

items.en: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.
items.explanation: *Katze* is feminine: **die Katze**. Many two-syllable nouns ending in *-e* are feminine (*die Katze, die Lampe, die Tasse*). This is a useful clue, but it has exceptions (*der Käse, der Name, das Auge*).

mistake.wrong: Der Katze schläft auf dem Sofa.
mistake.why: *Katze* is feminine. As the subject (Nominativ) it takes *die*, not *der*.

examples.de: Die Ente schwimmt auf dem See.
examples.en: The duck is swimming on the lake.

examples.de: Die Tasse steht auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The cup is on the table.

items.explanation: *Auto* is neuter: **das Auto** (short for *das Automobil*). Many nouns from other languages that end in *-o* are neuter: *das Auto, das Kino, das Radio, das Büro*. English speakers often guess *der* for things, but there is no such rule.

mistake.why: *Auto* is neuter, so the Nominativ article is *das*. Learn it as one unit: *das Auto*.

examples.de: Das Büro ist im ersten Stock.
examples.en: The office is on the first floor.

items.explanation: *Lehrer* is formed from the verb *lehren* + *-er* and names a male person who does something. These agent nouns are masculine: **der Lehrer**, *der Bäcker, der Fahrer*. The female form adds *-in* and is feminine: *die Lehrerin*.

mistake.why: *die Lehrer* is the plural (the teachers) and needs the verb *kommen*. For one male teacher the article is *der*.

examples.de: Der Bäcker backt jeden Morgen Brot.
examples.en: The baker bakes bread every morning.

examples.de: Der Fahrer wartet vor dem Hotel.
examples.en: The driver is waiting in front of the hotel.

items.explanation: *Schule* is feminine: **die Schule**. English says *School starts* without an article, but German uses the definite article for the school or the lessons people know: **Die** *Schule beginnt*. Without the article the sentence sounds incomplete.

mistake.wrong: Das Schule beginnt um acht Uhr.
mistake.why: *Schule* is feminine (a noun in *-e*), so the subject is *die Schule*. Note also that the article cannot be left out here, unlike in English.

examples.de: Die Arbeit beginnt um neun Uhr.

items.explanation: *Buch* is neuter: **das Buch**, plural *die Bücher*. Short everyday nouns like this give no clue from their form, so learn *das Buch* as one unit. It is the subject, so the article is in the Nominativ.

mistake.why: *Buch* is neuter, not masculine. The Nominativ article is *das*.

examples.de: Das Bild hängt an der Wand.
examples.en: The picture is hanging on the wall.

items.explanation: *Apfel* is masculine: **der Apfel**, plural *die Äpfel*. Many nouns ending in *-el* are masculine (*der Löffel, der Schlüssel*), but there are many feminine ones too (*die Gabel, die Kartoffel*), so check each word.

mistake.why: *Apfel* is masculine. One apple is *der Apfel*; *die* would only fit the plural *die Äpfel*.

examples.de: Der Schlüssel liegt auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The key is on the table.

items.explanation: *Lampe* is feminine: **die Lampe**, plural *die Lampen*. The adjective *kaputt* after *ist* has no ending, so in this sentence the article is the only word that shows the gender of the noun.

mistake.why: *Lampe* is feminine. As the subject it takes the feminine Nominativ article *die*.

examples.en: The washing machine is already old.

items.explanation: *Haus* is neuter: **das Haus**. It is the subject of *hat*, so it is in the Nominativ. Compare *einen Garten*: *der Garten* is the Akkusativ object of *haben*, so its article changes. The subject article does not change.

mistake.why: *Haus* is neuter, so the subject is *das Haus*. Do not take the gender from *Garten* (masculine) in the same sentence.

items.explanation: *Kaffee* is masculine: **der Kaffee**. Most hot drinks are masculine (*der Kaffee, der Tee, der Kakao*), and so are most alcoholic drinks (*der Wein, der Schnaps*). An important exception: *das Bier*.

mistake.why: *Kaffee* is masculine, so the subject is *der Kaffee*. *das* is only for neuter drinks such as *das Bier* or *das Wasser*.

items.explanation: *Tür* is feminine: **die Tür**, plural *die Türen*. One-syllable nouns give no reliable clue: *die Tür*, but *das Tor* (gate) and *der Zaun* (fence). Learn the article with the noun.

mistake.why: *Tür* is feminine. The masculine *der* is wrong for the subject; the Nominativ is *die Tür*.

examples.en: The post office is closed today.

examples.de: Die Bank ist bis 16 Uhr offen.
examples.en: The bank is open until 4 p.m.

items.explanation: *Mädchen* ends in the diminutive suffix *-chen*, and every noun in *-chen* is neuter, even when it names a girl: **das Mädchen**. The ending decides the grammatical gender, not the person.

mistake.why: *die Mädchen* is only possible as a plural (*Die Mädchen sind nett.*). In the singular, *-chen* always gives *das*.

examples.de: Das Häuschen am See ist sehr alt.
examples.en: The little house by the lake is very old.

examples.de: Das Kätzchen spielt mit dem Ball.
examples.en: The kitten is playing with the ball.

items.explanation: *Tisch* is masculine: **der Tisch**, plural *die Tische*. Many pieces of furniture are masculine (*der Tisch, der Stuhl, der Schrank*), but not all: *das Bett, das Sofa, die Couch*.

mistake.why: *Tisch* is masculine, so the Nominativ article is *der*. Things are not neuter by default.

items.explanation: *Sonne* is feminine in German: **die Sonne**, while *der Mond* is masculine. In many other languages it is the other way round, so do not transfer the gender from another language.

mistake.why: In German the sun is feminine: *die Sonne*. *der* belongs to *der Mond*.

examples.de: Die Luft ist heute sehr frisch.
examples.en: The air is very fresh today.

items.explanation: *Wetter* is neuter: **das Wetter**. It ends in *-er*, but the *-er* clue for masculine is reliable only for people and devices (*der Lehrer, der Drucker*). Other neuter nouns in *-er*: *das Fenster, das Zimmer, das Wasser*.

mistake.why: *Wetter* is neuter. The ending *-er* alone does not make a noun masculine; the clue is reliable only for people and devices.

items.explanation: *Kaffee* ends in *-e*, which can make learners guess feminine, but it is masculine: **der Kaffee** (like *der Tee* and *der See*, 'lake'). *Euro* is masculine as well, and in prices it has no plural ending: *zwei Euro*.

mistake.why: The final *-e* is not a feminine clue here. *Kaffee* is masculine: *der Kaffee*.

items.explanation: *Frage* comes from the verb *fragen* and is feminine: **die Frage**, plural *die Fragen*. Many nouns formed from a verb + *-e* are feminine: *reisen → die Reise, helfen → die Hilfe*.

mistake.why: *Frage* is feminine, so the subject article is *die*. Only the verb *fragen* has no gender.

items.explanation: *Fenster* is neuter: **das Fenster**, although *die Tür* is feminine. Similar things can have different genders. The plural is *die Fenster*, the same form as the singular, so only the article shows the number.

mistake.why: *Fenster* ends in *-er* but is neuter. The Nominativ singular is *das Fenster*.

examples.de: Das Geschäft ist bis 20 Uhr offen.
examples.en: The shop is open until 8 p.m.

items.explanation: *Park* is masculine: **der Park**, plural *die Parks*. Many places in a town are masculine (*der Park, der Platz, der Markt, der Bahnhof*), but many are not (*die Straße, das Zentrum*), so learn each one with its article.

mistake.why: *Park* is masculine, so the subject is *der Park*.

items.explanation: *Suppe* is feminine: **die Suppe** (a noun in *-e*). With *schmecken* the food is the subject, so it stands in the Nominativ: *Die Suppe schmeckt gut.*

mistake.why: *Suppe* is feminine, and as the subject of *schmeckt* it takes *die*.

items.explanation: Nouns ending in *-thek* are feminine: **die Bibliothek**, *die Mediathek*. Other reliable feminine endings are *-ung, -heit, -keit, -ion*. The adjective *geschlossen* after *ist* gives no help, so the ending is the clue.

mistake.why: The suffix *-thek* always gives a feminine noun, so the article is *die*.

examples.de: Die Apotheke ist am Sonntag geschlossen.
examples.en: The pharmacy is closed on Sunday.

items.explanation: Seasons, months and days of the week are masculine: **der Frühling**, *der März, der Montag*. English uses no article for seasons, but German says *der Frühling*. One exception: *das Frühjahr*, another word for spring.

mistake.why: All seasons are masculine: *der Frühling, der Sommer, der Herbst, der Winter*.

examples.de: Der Sommer ist hier sehr heiß.

items.en: The girl is waiting for the bus.
items.explanation: *Mädchen* is a diminutive (originally *Magd* + *-chen*), and diminutives in *-chen* and *-lein* are always neuter: **das Mädchen**. The verb *wartet* is singular, which confirms one girl. *auf den Bus* is a different phrase: *warten auf* + Akkusativ.

mistake.wrong: Die Mädchen wartet auf den Bus.
mistake.why: The real sex of the person does not decide the article. *die Mädchen* would be plural and need *warten*; one girl is *das Mädchen*.

examples.en: The rabbit is sitting in the garden.

items.explanation: The suffix *-heit* makes abstract nouns from adjectives, and they are always feminine: *frei → **die** Freiheit*. German uses the article with abstract nouns more often than English: *Die Freiheit ist wichtig* = *Freedom is important*.

mistake.why: *-heit* nouns are feminine without exception, so the article is *die*.

items.explanation: *Wasser* is neuter: **das Wasser**. There is no rule that substances in *-er* are neuter (*die Butter* is feminine, *der Zucker* masculine), so this gender must simply be learned. Many common neuter nouns end in *-er*: *das Wasser, das Messer, das Fenster, das Theater*.

mistake.why: *Wasser* is neuter. The ending *-er* is not a reliable masculine clue for things: *das Wasser*.

examples.en: The theatre is sold out today.

items.en: The computer is on the table.
items.explanation: Devices that do something and end in *-er* are usually masculine, like agent nouns for people: **der Computer**, *der Drucker, der Fernseher*. German often uses *stehen* for objects that are upright: *Der Computer steht auf dem Tisch.*

mistake.wrong: Das Computer steht auf dem Tisch.
mistake.why: *Computer* is a device in *-er*, and these are masculine: *der Computer*.

items.en: The newspaper is on the sofa.
items.explanation: Nouns formed with the suffix *-ung* are always feminine: **die Zeitung**, *die Wohnung, die Rechnung*. Words like *der Sprung* or *der Schwung* are not exceptions, because their *-ung* is not the suffix but part of the stem.

mistake.wrong: Der Zeitung liegt auf dem Sofa.
mistake.why: *Zeitung* ends in the suffix *-ung*, which always gives a feminine noun: *die Zeitung*.

examples.en: The invitation is in the letterbox.

items.en: The degree programme takes four years.
items.explanation: Latin loans in *-um* are neuter: **das Studium**, *das Museum, das Zentrum*. The German suffix *-tum* is a different case: it is usually neuter too (*das Eigentum, das Wachstum*), but *der Irrtum* and *der Reichtum* are masculine.

mistake.why: *Studium* is a Latin loan in *-um*, and these are neuter: *das Studium*.

examples.en: The museum is closed on Mondays.

items.en: The university is in the centre.
items.explanation: The ending *-tät* (from Latin *-tas*) always gives a feminine noun: **die Universität**, *die Qualität, die Nationalität*. *liegen* is the normal verb for the location of buildings and towns.

mistake.why: *-tät* nouns are feminine, so the subject is *die Universität*.

examples.en: The nationality is written in the passport.

items.explanation: *Käse* ends in *-e* but is masculine: **der Käse**, an exception to the *-e* → feminine tendency. Food shows that gender does not follow meaning: *der Käse, die Butter, das Brot*.

mistake.why: The final *-e* is misleading here. *Käse* is masculine: *der Käse*.

items.explanation: *Restaurant* is a French loan and neuter: **das Restaurant**. Loans in *-ment* are mostly neuter (*das Dokument, das Medikament*). The ending *-ant* gives no safe rule: *das Restaurant*, but *der Elefant, der Praktikant*.

mistake.why: *Restaurant* is neuter. The masculine *der* is wrong; the subject is *das Restaurant*.

examples.de: Das Café öffnet um acht Uhr.
examples.en: The café opens at eight o'clock.
The department store opens at ten.

items.explanation: In the plural all three genders take the same Nominativ article **die**: *das Kind → die Kinder*. The plural verb *spielen* also shows that the subject is plural.

mistake.why: *das* is only for the singular *das Kind*. In the plural the article is always *die*.

examples.en: The parents are working late today.

items.explanation: In a compound noun the **last** part (the Grundwort) decides the gender: *kühl + der Schrank → **der** Kühlschrank*. The first part only adds meaning: a cupboard that cools.
items.pattern: der + Kompositum (letzter Teil maskulin, Nom.) + ist + Adjektiv

mistake.why: The gender comes from the last part, *der Schrank*. So the whole word is *der Kühlschrank*.

examples.en: The main station is brand new.

items.en: The mobile phone is in the bag.
items.explanation: *Handy* is the German word for a mobile phone (it is not used this way in English), and it is neuter: **das Handy**. Many English loans are neuter (*das Hobby, das Baby, das Ticket*), but not all: *die Party, der Job*.

mistake.wrong: Der Handy liegt in der Tasche.
mistake.why: *Handy* is neuter: *das Handy*. English loans do not become masculine automatically.

examples.de: Das Ticket liegt auf dem Schreibtisch.
examples.en: The ticket is on the desk.
The baby is sleeping in the pram.

items.explanation: *-keit*, like *-heit*, forms feminine abstract nouns from adjectives: *möglich → **die** Möglichkeit*. *-keit* is used mainly after adjectives in *-lich, -ig, -bar*. *bestehen* here means 'to exist'; a very common fuller form is *Es besteht die Möglichkeit, dass …*.

mistake.why: Every noun in *-keit* is feminine, so the subject is *die Möglichkeit*.

examples.de: Die Pünktlichkeit ist im Job wichtig.
Die Sauberkeit im Hotel ist sehr gut.
examples.en: The cleanliness in the hotel is very good.

items.explanation: *Winter* is a season and therefore masculine: **der Winter**. Many weather words are masculine too (*der Regen, der Schnee, der Wind, der Nebel*), but not all: *das Wetter, das Gewitter, die Sonne, die Wolke*.

mistake.why: Seasons are masculine without exception (*das Frühjahr* is a separate word), so the article is *der*.

examples.de: Der Sommer war viel zu heiß.
examples.en: The summer was far too hot.

items.explanation: Nouns ending in *-ion* are feminine: **die Lektion**, *die Information, die Region, die Station*. The ending is stressed (*Lek-ti-ON*), which helps you hear it.

mistake.why: The ending *-ion* always gives a feminine noun, so the article is *die*.

items.en: The team is playing in Berlin today.
items.explanation: *Mannschaft* contains *der Mann*, but the suffix *-schaft* decides the gender, and *-schaft* nouns are always feminine: **die Mannschaft**. Other examples: *die Freundschaft, die Landschaft*.

mistake.wrong: Der Mannschaft spielt heute in Berlin.
mistake.why: The gender of *der Mann* does not count. The suffix *-schaft* makes the word feminine: *die Mannschaft*.

items.en: The doctor doesn't have time today.
items.explanation: *Ärztin* is the female form of *der Arzt*, made with the suffix *-in* (and an umlaut here). Every noun in *-in* for a female person is feminine: **die Ärztin**. The plural is *die Ärztinnen*.

mistake.wrong: Der Ärztin hat heute keine Zeit.
mistake.why: *der* belongs to the male form *der Arzt*. The form with *-in* is always feminine: *die Ärztin*.

examples.en: The teacher explains the grammar. (female teacher)
The shop assistant is helping us. (female)

items.en: The tourist is looking for the station.
items.explanation: Person nouns in *-ist* are masculine: **der Tourist**, *der Journalist, der Polizist*. The female form is *die Touristin*. *der Tourist* is the subject (Nominativ); *den Bahnhof* is the Akkusativ object of *suchen*.

mistake.why: One male tourist is *der Tourist*. A female tourist is *die Touristin*, and *die Touristen* is the plural.

examples.en: The journalist is writing an article.
The police officer is helping the man.

items.explanation: Many nouns that begin with *Ge-* are neuter: **das Gemüse**, *das Getränk, das Gebäude, das Geschenk*. Exceptions exist (*der Geburtstag, die Geschichte*). *Gemüse* is a singular collective noun, so English uses the plural *vegetables* but German uses the singular *ist*.

mistake.why: The final *-e* suggests feminine, but *Ge-* nouns like *Gemüse* are neuter: *das Gemüse*.

items.explanation: When an infinitive is used as a noun, it is always neuter and written with a capital letter: *essen → **das** Essen*. In the same way: *das Schwimmen, das Kochen, das Lernen*.

mistake.why: A noun made from an infinitive is always neuter: *das Essen*.

items.de: {{c1::Die::Artikel}} Person am Telefon ist mein Chef.
items.en: The person on the phone is my boss.
items.explanation: *Person* is always feminine, also when the person is a man: **die Person**. The grammatical gender belongs to the word. The man is named by *mein Chef* after *ist*, but the subject *die Person* keeps its own article.

mistake.wrong: Der Person am Telefon ist mein Chef.
mistake.why: The article does not follow the real person (a man). *Person* is a feminine word: *die Person*.

examples.de: Die Person vor mir ist sehr groß.
examples.en: The person in front of me is very tall.

items.en: What's the name of the man over there?
items.explanation: For most people the article follows the natural gender: **der Mann**, *der Vater, der Bruder*. In this W-question the subject stands after the verb *heißt*, but it is still the subject and therefore still Nominativ: *der*.

mistake.wrong: Wie heißt das Mann da drüben?
mistake.why: *Mann* is masculine, matching the natural gender. The subject is *der Mann*, also after the verb.

examples.en: Where does the waiter come from?

items.explanation: The first *Das* is a pointing word ('that') and never changes. The article of the noun comes from the last part of the compound: *der Bus + die Haltestelle → **die** Bushaltestelle*. So one sentence can contain *das* and *die* together.
items.pattern: Das ist + Artikel des letzten Wortteils + Kompositum

mistake.why: *der* comes from the first part *der Bus*. The last part, *die Haltestelle*, decides: *die Bushaltestelle*.

examples.de: Das ist der Schreibtisch von Anna.
Das ist die Telefonnummer von Tom.

items.en: The bakery opens at six o'clock.
items.explanation: Nouns ending in stressed *-ei* are feminine: **die Bäckerei**, *die Metzgerei, die Polizei*. Compare the person *der Bäcker* (masculine) with the shop *die Bäckerei* (feminine): the new suffix brings a new gender.

mistake.wrong: Der Bäckerei öffnet um sechs Uhr.
mistake.why: *der* belongs to *der Bäcker*. The suffix *-ei* makes the word feminine: *die Bäckerei*.

examples.en: The police are coming right away.

examples.de: Die Metzgerei ist gleich um die Ecke.
examples.en: The butcher's is just around the corner.

items.explanation: Nouns ending in *-ik* are feminine: **die Musik**, *die Physik, die Technik, die Politik*. In a yes/no question the verb *ist* comes first, but *die Musik* is still the subject in the Nominativ.

mistake.why: *-ik* nouns are feminine. *das* is wrong here; the subject is *die Musik*.

items.explanation: *der Schlüssel* has the same form in the plural: *die Schlüssel*. Here only the article **die** and the plural verb *sind* show that there are several keys. In the plural every noun takes *die* in the Nominativ.

mistake.why: *der Schlüssel* is singular. With *sind* the subject is plural, and the plural article is *die*.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about grammatical gender.
drills.prompt: Why should you always learn a German noun together with its article?
drills.answer: Because the gender (**der/die/das**) is a property of the word and usually cannot be guessed from its meaning. Many later forms depend on it: *den/dem/des*, adjective endings and the pronouns *er/sie/es*.
drills.explanation: Similar things often have different genders: *der Löffel, die Gabel, das Messer*. Some endings help, but many everyday nouns have no clue. Learning *der Tisch* as one unit is faster than guessing every time.

examples.en: The spoon is on the left.
The fork is on the right.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about feminine endings.
drills.prompt: Which noun endings tell you that a noun is feminine?
drills.answer: **-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät, -ei, -ik, -thek** and **-in** for female persons. Many nouns in *-e* are also feminine, but that clue has exceptions.
drills.explanation: The suffixes *-ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -ion, -tät* are practically without exceptions. The ending *-e* is only a tendency: *die Lampe*, but *der Käse, der Name, das Auge*.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about neuter nouns.
drills.prompt: Which groups of nouns are neuter?
drills.answer: Diminutives in **-chen / -lein**, infinitives used as nouns (*das Essen*), Latin loans in **-um** (*das Museum*), most loans in **-ment**, and many nouns with **Ge-** (*das Gemüse*).
drills.explanation: *-chen* and *-lein* always give *das*, even for people (*das Mädchen*). Nominalised infinitives are always neuter. The *Ge-* rule has exceptions such as *der Geburtstag* and *die Geschichte*.

examples.en: The bread roll is still warm.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about masculine nouns.
drills.prompt: Which groups of nouns are usually masculine?
drills.answer: Male persons (*der Vater*), days, months and seasons (*der Montag, der Mai, der Winter*), many weather words (*der Regen, der Schnee*), nouns in **-ling, -ismus, -ist**, and people or devices in **-er** (*der Lehrer, der Drucker*).
drills.explanation: The *-er* clue is reliable only for people and devices; things like *das Fenster* or *das Wasser* are neuter. Weather words are mixed: *das Wetter, die Sonne*.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about compound nouns.
drills.prompt: Which part of a compound noun decides its article?
drills.answer: The **last** part (the Grundwort): *das Haus + die Tür → **die** Haustür*; *schlafen + das Zimmer → **das** Schlafzimmer*.
drills.explanation: The first part only describes the last part more exactly. It can be a noun, a verb stem or an adjective, but its gender never counts. The plural also comes from the last part: *die Haustüren*.

drills.instruction: Answer the question about the plural.
drills.prompt: Which definite article do plural nouns take in the Nominativ?
drills.answer: Always **die**, for masculine, feminine and neuter nouns: *der Mann → die Männer, die Frau → die Frauen, das Kind → die Kinder*.
drills.explanation: The plural has no gender distinction. Because feminine singular is also *die*, look at the noun and the verb to see the number: *Die Frau ist …* vs *Die Frauen sind …*.

examples.de: Die Bücher liegen auf dem Tisch.
examples.en: The books are on the table.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct article.
drills.answer: Die Wohnung ist leider zu teuer.
drills.explanation: *Wohnung* ends in the suffix *-ung*, which always gives a feminine noun: *die Wohnung*. *Der* would be masculine and *Das* neuter; neither fits an *-ung* noun.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct article.
drills.explanation: *Würstchen* is the diminutive of *die Wurst*, and every noun in *-chen* is neuter: *das Würstchen*. *Die* would come from *die Wurst*, but the suffix *-chen* changes the gender. *Der* has no basis here.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct article.
drills.prompt: ___ Tourismus ist wichtig für die Stadt.
drills.answer: Der Tourismus ist wichtig für die Stadt.
drills.explanation: Nouns ending in *-ismus* are masculine: *der Tourismus, der Journalismus*. *Die* and *Das* are wrong for this ending.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct article.
drills.explanation: *Geschenk* starts with *Ge-* and, like many such nouns, is neuter: *das Geschenk*. *Der* and *Die* do not fit this word.

drills.instruction: Choose the correct article.
drills.prompt: ___ Häuser in der Altstadt sind sehr alt.
drills.answer: Die Häuser in der Altstadt sind sehr alt.
drills.explanation: *Häuser* is the plural of *das Haus*, and the verb *sind* is plural. Every plural noun takes *die*. *Das* is only for the singular *das Haus*, and *Der* fits neither form.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.explanation: The mistake is the article. *Mädchen* ends in *-chen*, so it is neuter: *das Mädchen*. The real sex of the child does not decide the article.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.explanation: The mistake is the article. Nouns in *-ion* are feminine, so the subject is *die Information*.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.explanation: The mistake: the article was taken from the first part, *das Haus*. In a compound the last part decides, and *die Aufgabe* is feminine: *die Hausaufgabe*.

drills.instruction: Find and correct the mistake.
drills.explanation: The mistake: the singular article *das* (from *das Buch*) is used with a plural noun. In the plural the Nominativ article is always *die*.

drills.instruction: Replace *Lampe* with *Licht*. Adjust the article.
drills.explanation: *Lampe* is feminine (*die*), but *Licht* is neuter: *das Licht*. The rest of the sentence stays the same, because the adjective after *ist* has no ending.

drills.instruction: Make the subject plural (*der Stuhl → die Stühle*). Change the verb.
drills.explanation: In the plural the masculine *der* becomes *die*, the noun gets its plural form with umlaut (*Stühle*), and the verb changes from *ist* to *sind*.

drills.instruction: Replace *der Lehrer* with the female form. Adjust the article.
drills.explanation: The female form adds *-in*: *Lehrer → Lehrerin*. Every noun in *-in* for a female person is feminine, so *der* changes to *die*.

drills.instruction: Put the parts in the correct order. Start with: Heute
drills.explanation: *Heute* is in position 1, so the verb *ist* follows in position 2 and the subject *das Museum* comes after it. *Museum* is a Latin loan in *-um* and neuter. The other correct order is *Das Museum ist heute geschlossen.*

drills.instruction: Put the parts in order to make a W-question.
drills.explanation: The question word *wo* is in position 1 and the verb *ist* in position 2. *Toilette* is feminine (a noun in *-e*), so the subject is *die Toilette*.
